extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, anatomists, and physicians (17th‑century scientific readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for observing, experimenting, and reporting natural‑philosophy/medical phenomena (tides, anatomy, hearing, vision, transfusion). Emphasises experimental method, observational repetition, simple apparatus, and cautious interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tide time prediction — circular proportion method
rubrics_metrics.description: A procedural rule to find the true time of high tide between new/full moon and the quarters by representing the moon's motion on a circle and using a diameter divided into minutes corresponding to tidal difference (one hour and a half = 90 minutes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps: divide a circle into 12 equal parts (hours) according to the moon's motion from new to full; divide the diameter into 90 parts (minutes) representing the tide-time difference between new/full and quarters; draw perpendicular lines from each hour to the diameter; locate the moon's southing point on the circumference and read off the perpendicular intersection on the diameter to find minutes to subtract from high‑tide time at new/full moon. Example: for London (high tide at new/full = 3:00), when the moon southing corresponds to perpendicular that cuts diameter at 45 min, subtract 45 min to get actual high tide (5:15 instead of 6:00 by common rule). Recommendation: make a table indexed by moon southing to read high tide times readily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical validation by repeated trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Refine rules and detect non-uniform patterns by many repeated observations across lunar phases rather than relying on coarse or single-instance rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes finding the tidal timing rule only after 'many trials' and emphasises that the variation between new/full and quarters is not linear or constant. Perform numerous observations across the moon's cycle and record deviations (e.g., greatest difference mid‑way between phases) before adopting a predictive rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing tympanum function in deafness
rubrics_metrics.description: When diagnosing congenital or acquired deafness, evaluate the physical state and tension of the tympanic membrane and the integrity of the auditory nerve; laxity of the tympanum can deaden sound even when the nerve remains intact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests: check bone conduction (e.g., sound transmitted via a lute‑string held in teeth) to assess auditory nerve; inspect ear passages for blockage or tympanum laxity; consider that a tense, hard‑stretched tympanum allows free passage of sound while laxity dampens it. Remedies: consult learned physicians; if tympanum perforation risks later impairment from cold, introduce wool or cotton into ear cavity to counteract. Do not assume nerve destruction without testing for residual perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating the optic‑nerve blind spot (Mariotte/Picard methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple visual experiments to show a locus where no distinct vision occurs (the blind spot) by arranging targets and directing fixation so the image falls on the optic nerve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monocular method (Mariotte): fix a point and place a second paper laterally; with one eye open and the other shut, move away until the lateral paper disappears, showing a blind area; vary distances to see individual differences. Binocular method (Picard): place two marks to left/right of a central paper and position a finger so each eye is occluded for the opposite mark; looking steadily at the finger can make the central paper disappear with both eyes open. Interpretation: vary distances and positions; blind‑spot size and location vary between observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of alternative anatomical explanations for experimental observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Before drawing mechanistic conclusions from sensory or anatomical experiments, consider confounding anatomical structures (e.g., large trunks of retinal vessels) that could produce the observed effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pecquet's reply cautions that the apparent loss of an image may be caused by large trunks of the vessels of the retina/retinal vessels intercepting the image rather than proving that vision is not in the retina. Always evaluate whether vascular trunks, membrane placement (choroides vs retina), or other anatomical features could account for a blind area; do not abandon prevailing hypotheses without excluding such alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of injections and transfusions to probe anatomical connectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Injecting liquids into vessels/organs can reveal internal communications and flow‑paths (e.g., injection into the vas deferens demonstrates filling of vesiculae seminales before any fluid reaches the urethra).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design injections to reveal directional connectivity and bottlenecks (e.g., anatomical angles that require upstream compartments to fill first). Prepare drawings/figures of the anatomy and report whether injected fluid reaches target compartments; interpret results in light of anatomical geometry (angles, junctions) rather than assuming direct passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in translating animal infusion/transfusion results to human therapeutics
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments that infuse various liquors into the veins of animals may be informative anatomically but are not automatically indicative of safe or effective human medical treatments; special circumstances (e.g., massive haemorrhage) may be the only justified therapeutic use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations: infusion into animals can restore apparent vigour (example: an animal bled to convulsions recovered within minutes after transfusion), but the author doubts general usefulness and safety for treating diseases or restoring youth in aged humans. Consider that infused nutritive/medicated liquids must undergo normal concoction/metabolic changes before mixing with blood to be beneficial. Weigh benefits against safety and species differences; use evidence from repeated experiments and witnesses when claiming therapeutic applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer function or multiple materials from structural and compositional differences
rubrics_metrics.description: When anatomical parts differ in structure, colour, or consistence, infer that they may produce or contain different materials or have different functions (e.g., testicle, epididymis, prostate producing different components of seminal fluid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare textures, colours and the anatomical relationship of parts. Use dissections and injections to corroborate functional inferences rather than relying solely on appearance. Report differences clearly and cautiously: structural variation supports (but does not alone prove) distinct material origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document priority, dates, and reproducibility when claiming discoveries
rubrics_metrics.description: When asserting discovery or priority of an experimental technique or anatomical finding, provide precise dates, multiple repetitions, and corroborating witnesses or publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dr. Clarck corrects the record about the dates and locations of infusion experiments and cites witnesses and publications. To support priority claims, include contemporaneous documentation, repeat the experiments when possible, and note others' prior or independent observations to situate the claim accurately.
